8	### Question
9	What is the absolute cheapest car to **own** over 10 years, all-in, buying **used**, driving ~12,000 mi/yr, based in Kansas City? Cost = purchase + fuel/electricity + maintenance/repair + insurance + registration/taxes, net of what the car is worth at the end.
10	
11	### Bottom line
12	- **Lowest cost on paper:** Nissan Leaf (~$50k / 10 yrs) — but only if its battery is healthy and stays that way. Big tail risk.
13	- **Lowest *risk-adjusted* cost (the real winner):** **Chevy Bolt EV with a recall-replaced battery** (~$52k / 10 yrs, ~$0.43/mi). Active battery cooling + a fresh warranted pack from the recall = the EV fuel/maintenance savings without the Leaf's degradation gamble. **Requires home charging.**
14	- **Cheapest gas car to own (no charging needed):** **Honda Fit or Kia Rio** (~$56k). Toyota Corolla is ~$58k but buys the lowest repair risk in the field.
15	- **The trap:** Mitsubishi Mirage is the cheapest car to *buy* ($7.5k) but one of the more expensive to *own* (~$57k) — it insures like a much pricier car and saves little on fuel.
16	
17	### The dominant cost is NOT purchase price
18	Over 10 years the order of magnitude is: **Insurance (~$18–25k) > Fuel (~$5–15k) ≈ Purchase (~$8–20k) ≈ Maintenance (~$6–12k) > Taxes/fees (~$2.5–5.5k).** Purchase price is only ~15–30% of the total. Here's the verdict, measured against the research we did May 28.

## Is it a good deal?

**Yes — cautiously. This is close to the car our research said was nearly impossible to find.**

The single biggest finding in the [Used Prius Buying Guide](/Users/alexhedtke/Exobrain/Research/Used%20Prius%20Buying%20Guide%20(Under%20%2410k,%20KC).md) was the **liftback budget-vs-mileage squeeze**: under $10k *and* under ~150k miles "barely overlap." Cheap liftbacks ($5–7k) all had **180k–260k miles**; the low-mileage ones commanded **$13–16k** (our Candidate 2 was a 62k-mile 2010 liftback at $15,988).

This car breaks that squeeze:
- **114k miles** sits right in our defined **sweet spot (100k–140k)** and well under the **160k hard cap**.
- **$7,900 OBO** is sub-$10k. A low-mileage liftback at this price is the unicorn the research said didn't exist locally.

## On price specifically

KBB private-party for a 2011 Prius **Two** in *good* condition is **~$6,400–7,200**, and that's at typical mileage. At 114k miles it lands near the top of that band. So $7,900 is **a touch above private-party book but in dealer-asking territory** — and it's **OBO**, which is the whole game.

- Open around **$6,800–7,000**, settle **~$7,200**.
- Walk-away leverage: the looming battery age (below).

## The two things that decide it (don't skip)

1. **EGR / head-gasket risk** — this is the Gen 3 liftback's *one real weak spot* (the Prius C dodges it; the liftback doesn't). **Demand documented EGR/intake cleaning records.** No records = assume it's due and price/negotiate accordingly.
2. **Battery age** — a 2011 at 114k almost certainly has its **original 15-year-old pack**. That's caveat #6 in the TCO note. A replacement runs **~$1,500–2,500**. **Run a Dr. Prius scan (OBD2 dongle, ~10 min) before paying — no exceptions.** A healthy pack makes $7,900 fair; a tired one means you negotiate hard or walk.
3. Plus the basics: clean title + VIN check for salvage/flood/hail.

## How it compares to the Prius C we were leaning toward

| | This 2011 liftback | Candidate 1 (2012 Prius C) |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $7,900 OBO | $6,585 (target ~$5k) |
| Miles | **114k** ✅ sweet spot | 155k (over our 160k caution) |
| Battery | Original, 15 yr — **unknown** | **Already replaced** at 100k (~55k on it) ✅ |
| EGR risk | **Yes** — screen for it | No ✅ |
| Car | Roomier, better highway ✅ | Small, basic, dinged (roof dent, stains) |
| Condition | Unknown (clean per listing) | Fair/beater-grade |

**Net:** The C's killer advantage was *the battery's already done* — the expensive risk paid down. This liftback gives you the **better car at far better mileage**, but you're **buying the battery risk back**. If the Dr. Prius scan comes back healthy and there are EGR-service records, this is the **stronger buy** and worth the extra ~$2k over the C. If the battery's tired with no service history, the C is the safer dollar.

Want me to draft the seller message — asking for service records (EGR especially), battery history, and clean-title confirmation, plus a soft opening offer?

Good news up front: **Jackson County doesn't require an emissions test** (that's only the St. Louis metro). But two MO quirks matter for *this specific car*, flagged below.

## The actual cash-exchange day

**Meet at a bank** — ideally the seller's or yours, mid-day. You verify and count the cash (or hand over a cashier's check) at the teller window, and the title gets signed right there. Don't release a dollar until the title is signed over in front of you. A bank also lets the seller confirm the bills are real. (KCPD and many suburbs also have marked "safe exchange" lots, but a bank is better here because you can verify funds.)

## What the SELLER must hand you / do

1. **The Certificate of Title, properly assigned** — this is the whole ballgame. Seller fills in the assignment on the back: your name, the **sale price**, **date**, and the **odometer reading**, then signs. Confirm the name on the title matches their ID.
2. **Lien release (Form 4809)** — if the title shows any lienholder, you need a notarized release proving it's paid off. If the title isn't clean and lien-free, **walk** until it is.
3. **Safety inspection certificate, less than 60 days old** ⚠️ — **this car is not exempt.** MO exempts cars only in their first 10 model years *and* under 150k miles; a 2011 is 15 years old, so a valid MO safety inspection is **required to title it.** Either the seller provides a current certificate, or you build "subject to passing a safety inspection (~$12 at any MO station)" into the deal. Don't skip this — without it the license office won't title the car.
4. **Bill of Sale (Form 1957)** — signed by both of you: VIN, year/make, price, date, odometer, both names/signatures. This is your receipt and the DOR's tax basis.
5. **Both keys/fobs, and they remove their license plates** — in Missouri **plates stay with the seller** (they transfer them to another car or surrender them). The car leaves with you plate-less.

## What the SELLER must do to protect themselves (and you should confirm they will)

- **File a Notice of Sale (Form 5049) with the DOR within 30 days.** This releases them from liability for anything you do with the car afterward (tickets, tolls, a crash). It's their protection, but you want them to do it so they have no reason to dispute the sale later.

## What YOU (the buyer) must do

1. **Get insurance on the car before you drive it off** — bind a policy with the VIN first. You need proof of insurance to title and to be legal on the road.
2. **Drive it home legally** — either put plates you already own on it, or get a **temporary operating permit** (DOR, when you apply) to cover you until titling.
3. **Title it within 30 days** at any MO license office (Jackson County has several). Bring:
   - The assigned title + Bill of Sale (Form 1957)
   - The **safety inspection certificate**
   - **Form 108 (Title Application)** — you fill this out in the office
   - Proof of insurance + your ID
4. **Pay at the counter:** state sales tax **4.225%** + Jackson County/KC local tax (combined roughly **7.5–9%** depending on your exact city — on $7,200 that's ~$540–650), plus title fee (~$8.50), registration, and a processing fee. The office calculates the exact local rate for your address.

⚠️ **Don't blow the 30-day window** — it's a $25 penalty on day 31, +$25 every 30 days after, up to $200. Title it the first week.

## The two-sided "make sure they..." checklist

**You make sure the seller:** has the title *in their own name*, signs/assigns it fully with odometer + price, the title is clean (not salvage/rebuilt/flood — verify on the VIN check) and lien-free, gives you the Bill of Sale and a current safety inspection, and hands over both keys.

**The seller makes sure you:** pay the full agreed amount in verified funds, sign the Bill of Sale, and take the car so they can pull their plates — and they should file the Notice of Sale so they're off the hook for liability.

A clean private sale is really just: **verified money ⇄ signed title + bill of sale + safety cert, done at a bank, then you title within 30 days.** The only non-obvious trap for this car is the **mandatory safety inspection** because it's over 10 years old.

## Option 1: Temporary Operating Permit (the "30-day tag")

**What it is:** a paper permit taped in the rear window that lets you legally drive a just-purchased car for **30 days** while you arrange titling. It's the bridge between "I just bought it, no plates" and "it's titled and registered in my name." One per vehicle, and it **becomes void the moment you apply for the title** — so it's not a way to delay titling, just to be legal in the meantime.

**Cost:** **$14** total — $5 permit fee + $9 processing — at any MO license office.

**How to get it** — walk into any Missouri license office with:
- The **Certificate of Title signed over to you** (or the bill of sale)
- **Form 108** (Application for Title and License)
- A **safety inspection certificate <60 days old** ⚠️ (required — see the catch below)
- **Proof of insurance** (card, photo, or electronic)

## Option 2: Transfer plates you already own

If you **already own another MO-registered vehicle** with valid plates, you can move those plates straight onto the Prius — no temp tag needed. Missouri plates belong to the *person*, not the car.

**How:** same license-office visit, same documents as above (assigned title, Form 108, safety inspection, insurance). You'd typically just title and register in one trip and ride on your existing plate. (This only works if you have a registered car to pull plates from — if the Prius is your only/first car, this isn't available and you want Option 1 or new plates.)

**Option 3** is just buying brand-new plates = full registration on the spot, which is what you'll end up doing within 30 days regardless.

## ⚠️ The catch that decides your path

Look at the document list — **every option requires the safety inspection certificate first**, because the 2011 is ~15 years old (MO only exempts cars under ~11 years old *and* under 150k miles). That creates a chicken-and-egg: you can't legally get a permit/plates without an inspection, but you need to move the car to get it inspected.

**The clean fix: make a current safety inspection a condition of the sale.** Ask the seller to get it inspected (~$12, any MO station) within 60 days of your purchase, or knock it out together before money changes hands. Then on buy-day you walk into the license office with the inspection already in hand and get your temp permit (or transfer plates) immediately — fully legal to drive home.

If the seller won't, your fallback for the very first drive (seller → inspection station) is to **trailer/tow it** or have a friend follow — driving an unplated, uninspected car on public roads is the one gray-area step worth not improvising.

The key thing nobody tells you: **you don't bring the car to the license office — you bring paperwork.** Titling and the temp permit are a desk transaction. So the car can sit parked the entire time you're doing the bureaucracy. That collapses the problem to one short hop.

Here's the cleanest physical sequence:

**1. Insure it first.** Bind a policy on the VIN before you touch the car. (Phone call to your agent on buy-day morning.)

**2. Get the inspection done while it's still legally drivable — i.e., before you pay.** This is the move that removes all the pain. Ask the seller to run it through a MO safety inspection station (~$12) as a sale condition, or meet them at a station before the handoff. While the car still has the **seller's plates on it**, *they* can legally drive it to the station. Once you've paid and the plates come off, that easy option is gone.

**3. Pay at the bank. Leave the car parked there (or at the seller's, or a friend's).** Don't drive it yet. It has no plates, but that's fine — it's just sitting.

**4. Take the paperwork — not the car — to a license office** in your own vehicle or with a ride. Buy the **$14 temp permit** (or transfer your existing plates). Five-minute desk transaction.

**5. Go back, tape the permit in the window, and now drive it home fully legal.**

That's it. The car never moves under its own power without either the seller's plates (steps before payment) or your permit (after step 4).

**The one leg to plan for:** getting the car from the seller's spot to wherever it'll park while you run paperwork. Three ways, cleanest first:
- **Park it at the seller's or a nearby lot** and leave it — then you're only driving it once, after you have the permit. Zero gray area.
- **Flatbed/tow it home** (AAA, U-Haul auto transport) if you can't leave it and don't want to drive it plate-less. Most conservative.
- **The short plate-less drive** that many private buyers just... do, same-day to the office area. Low practical risk, but it's not strictly legal and your fresh insurance is the only thing protecting you if something happens.

**Bottom line:** if you arrange the inspection *before* payment and leave the car parked while you grab the permit, the car only ever drives legally — once at the start (seller's plates, to inspection) and once at the end (your permit, home). The middle is all paperwork on foot. Do it all in one afternoon and you're never sitting on an undriveable car.

text: I do not currently own a car, so I need to get fresh plates.

blocks.text:
Right — no existing plates to fall back on, so the plan simplifies to one decision: **do everything in a single office trip and walk out with permanent metal plates.** Missouri license offices issue standard plates over the counter, so there's no reason to bother with the $14 temp permit in your case. You title, pay tax, register, and get plates in one sitting.

Your only real constraints are (a) the car needs a safety inspection before it can be plated, and (b) you have no car to get yourself around. Both are solvable in one afternoon **if you bring a friend with a car** (or budget for Ubers). Here's the concrete choreography:

**The one-day plan:**

1. **Morning — bind insurance** on the VIN by phone. (You can't register without it, and you want coverage before the car is yours anyway.)

2. **Meet the seller at a safety inspection station**, not at the bank. Tons of KC shops do MO inspections. The seller's plates are still on the car, so they can legally drive it there (or you both arrive and they pull in). Get the **~$12 safety inspection** done *before* you pay — while it's still their car on their plates.

3. **If it passes, drive to a nearby bank** (seller driving, still their plates) and do the money: verified cash ⇄ signed title + bill of sale. Seller removes their plates and leaves.

4. **Leave the Prius parked at the bank.** It's yours now but plate-less — don't drive it. Your friend drives you (or Uber) to a **license office** with:
   - Assigned title + bill of sale
   - **Form 108** (fill out there)
   - **Safety inspection certificate**
   - **Insurance card** + your **ID**
   - **Money for tax + fees** — sales tax (~7.5–9% of price, so ~$540–700 on a $7.2k car), title fee (~$8.50), registration, and plate fee. Bring a card or cash; confirm the office's payment methods.

5. **Title + register + get plates over the counter.** Friend drives you back to the parked Prius, you mount the plates, and drive home **fully legal.**

That's the whole thing — the car only ever moves on the seller's plates (to inspection) and then on your new plates (home). Zero plate-less driving, no temp permit, no 30-day clock hanging over you.

**If you can't compress it to one day** (e.g., you buy in the evening, offices closed): then buy the **$14 temp permit** at the office the next morning so you can drive the Prius home in the meantime — but you'd still have to get to the office without the car first, so honestly the cleaner fallback is to just **leave the Prius parked at the seller's overnight** and finish at the office the next day. Don't drive it on no plates to "save a trip."

**The honest friction for you:** with no car, the logistics hinge on having a ride for the bank→office→bank loop. Line that up in advance — a friend for the afternoon, or accept ~$30–40 in Ubers. That's the real thing to plan, not the paperwork.

Want me to build the day-of packet now — bill of sale to fill in, the document checklist for the office, and the insurance/inspection call list — as a single page in your Downloads?

text: Does this have to be done at a bank? What if we do the sale in the parking lot of the title office?

blocks.text:
No, the bank isn't required — and doing the sale in the **title office parking lot is actually the smartest version for your situation.** It solves your no-car logistics problem better than the bank does.

The bank was only ever there for one reason: a teller to verify and count the cash. That's a convenience, not a legal requirement. The title office lot gives you something more valuable: **the car is already exactly where it needs to be.** You sign, walk inside, title + register + get plates, walk back out, mount them, and drive home — no bank→office→bank shuttle, no leaving the car parked across town, no begging a friend for a multi-stop ride. The Prius just sits in the lot for the 20 minutes you're at the counter.

So the sequence becomes beautifully tight:

1. **Inspection done beforehand** ⚠️ — this is the one thing that still has to happen first. The office can't title the car without a safety inspection certificate in hand, and the car is too old to be exempt. So get it inspected a day or two earlier (it's valid 60 days), with the seller driving it on their plates to a station. *This is the only step that can't happen in the lot.*
2. **Meet at the title office lot.** Verify the cash, both sign the title assignment + bill of sale, seller pulls their plates and leaves.
3. **Walk inside** with title, bill of sale, inspection cert, Form 108, insurance card, ID, and your tax+fee money. Title, register, buy plates over the counter.
4. **Mount plates in the lot, drive home legal.** Done.

Two things to handle since you lose the bank teller:

- **Cash verification.** Bring a **counterfeit-detection pen** ($5) and count carefully, or — cleaner — withdraw the cash at your own bank earlier and bring a **cashier's check** made out to the seller instead (most private sellers accept one, and it sidesteps the "is this real" dance entirely). Decide with the seller in advance which they want.
- **Timing.** Go on a weekday with enough runway before the office closes, and confirm that specific office's hours and payment methods (some MO contract offices add a card fee — cash or check for the tax/fees may save you money).

One honest caveat: a few sellers are wary of counting a cash stack in a parking lot and will insist on a bank for *their* peace of mind. If yours does, no problem — but if they're flexible, the title office lot is the move. Float it to them as "let's just meet at the license office so we can do it all in one stop."

So: inspection first (separate, earlier), then everything else in one stop at the title office. That's the cleanest path for someone without a car to shuttle around in.

No, there's no pre-authorization feature, and the limits make Venmo a dead end for this anyway. Here's the wall you'd hit:

**Even fully identity-verified, a single Venmo payment to a person caps at $4,999.99.** The $60,000 figure you may have seen is a *weekly* rolling total, not a per-payment limit. So a $7,200 car physically cannot go in one Venmo transfer — you'd have to split it into two payments across the transaction. And "verifying" your identity (SSN, etc.) is the only lever to raise limits; there's no way to call ahead and authorize a one-time larger payment.

**Splitting it is exactly what gets accounts frozen.** Two large back-to-back transfers to a new recipient is textbook "unusual activity" — Venmo can freeze either account and hold the funds for review for *weeks*, often mid-sale. That's the seller's nightmare scenario, and they may refuse for that reason alone.

**The reversal risk is the real killer.** There's a documented case of a seller who signed over the title, helped the buyer get tags, and 12 hours later got an email that Venmo had *reversed the payment*. Venmo P2P has essentially no protection for vehicle sales — its own terms steer you away from buying from strangers. For you as the buyer it's less risk than the seller, but a savvy seller won't accept it, and you don't want your own funds locked either.

**What to use instead — and it fits the title-office-lot plan perfectly:**

- **Cashier's check** ✅ — the right tool for ~$7k. Get it from your bank made out to the seller's name. The seller can verify it by phoning the issuing bank, it can't bounce or be reversed like a Venmo transfer, there's a paper trail for your title/tax paperwork, and there's nothing to count in a parking lot. This is the clean move.
- **Cash** — also fine and final; just means counting/verifying in the lot (counterfeit pen).
- **Wire or Zelle** — wires work for large sums but need both parties at their banks; Zelle has its own per-day caps (often $1–2.5k for newer recipients) so it hits the same splitting problem.

For your one-stop-at-the-title-office plan, **walk in with a cashier's check.** You go to your bank a day before (you're going there anyway to pull the funds), get the check, and the parking-lot handoff becomes: hand over check, sign title, walk inside. No app limits, no freeze risk, no reversal.
